appraisal_events.evidence: The grandfather's cutting reply to Luxembourg's snub is judged to show "plus d'esprit que son petit-gendre"; the duchesse's own anecdotes of snubbing him and outmaneuvering him by phone make "tout le monde" laugh.
appraisal_events.explanation: Both the grandfather's story and the duchesse's own anecdotes stage M. de Luxembourg losing repeated wit contests before an amused room, though the narrator flags these very stories as likely "mensonges" born of Faubourg malice.

appraisal_events.evidence: "d'homme plus intelligent, meilleur, plus fin, tranchons le mot, plus exquis que ce Luxembourg-Nassau, je n'en ai jamais rencontré. La suite montrera que c'était moi qui avais raison."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly and emphatically overrides the salon's mockery, asserting his own strongly positive judgment of the man the room has just been ridiculing.

appraisal_events.evidence: M. de Guermantes' genealogical conversation is likened to an old house with "pas de chefs-d'œuvre véritables, mais pleine de tableaux authentiques, médiocres et majestueux, dont l'ensemble a grand air."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's simile frames the duc's command of family history as authentic yet individually mediocre, an impressive cumulative effect built from unremarkable parts.

status_effects.explanation: He is twice bested in wit before an audience that laughs at his expense, in stories the room accepts uncritically.
Her anecdotes of snubbing and outmaneuvering Luxembourg win the room's laughter, marking her as the scene's dominant wit.
The narrator's own emphatic judgment, made independently of the mocking anecdotes, rates him as exceptionally intelligent and refined.
The narrator's backhanded simile credits his genealogical talk with an impressive overall effect while explicitly denying it any real distinction piece by piece.

ambiguities: The narrator explicitly disbelieves the anecdotes mocking M. de Luxembourg and states his own contrary judgment will later be vindicated, so the salon's ridicule and the narrator's private assessment point in opposite directions for the same character.
